subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Fast and Frugal in the Real World
description: A 60-second lesson on Fast and Frugal in the Real World.

hook.text: A firefighter orders his team out of a building seconds before it collapses. He can't explain how he knew.

buildup.text: Klein's research on expert intuition shows that pattern recognition built from experience is genuinely fast.

discovery.text: In familiar domains with fast feedback, heuristics aren't flaws. They're evolved solutions to real problems.

twist.text: The same intuition fails in novel, slow-feedback domains like investing or hiring. Context determines value.

climax.text: The question isn't 'are heuristics good or bad?' It's 'does this environment match this shortcut?'

punchline.text: Right shortcut, right place. That's wisdom.

quiz.question: When do heuristics work well?
options: In familiar domains with fast feedback
Only when we have perfect information

details.summary: Fast-and-frugal heuristics use minimal information to make surprisingly accurate decisions in real-world environments. Rather than gathering all available data, these simple rules exploit the structure of the environment to achieve good outcomes with a fraction of the effort.
details.whyItMatters: Fast-and-frugal research shows that more information and computation do not always improve decisions. In many environments, simple rules match or outperform complex models because they are robust to noise and overfitting in uncertain worlds.
takeaways: Simple heuristics can match or exceed complex models in uncertain environments
Less information sometimes produces better decisions by avoiding overfitting
The environment's structure determines which heuristic is ecologically rational

faq.question: How can simpler decision rules outperform complex analysis?
faq.answer: Complex models fit past data precisely, including noise. In uncertain environments, this overfitting hurts prediction. Simple heuristics ignore noise by using less information, making them more robust when predicting new, unseen situations.

faq.question: What is an example of a fast-and-frugal heuristic?
faq.answer: Hospital emergency rooms use fast-and-frugal decision trees: check one symptom, then one more, and decide. These simple trees match the accuracy of complex regression models for heart-attack triage while being fast enough for real-time medical decisions.
